If the page you are watching HIMYM has a "like this show/site on Facebook" or anything like that, then yes FB would know.

Also, you don't have to be "logged into FB" for your data profile to start being built. Being "logged in" means you can admin your FB account. It doesn't have anything to do with being tracked or not.

Take for instance google. ANY page that runs google adsense or google analytics (which is the vast majority of the internet), google knows you visited that page no matter who administers or hosts the actual website.

With privacy addons, when you visit "Joe's Wordpress Homepage" and the page tries to call Google's adsense/analytics servers, the addon will block those third-party tracking calls so google won't know you visited that site. With privacy addons, you can only really be tracked by Google when you specifically visit their first-party services (eg; Youtube, Gmail, etc).

what information exactly can the companies collect about you

How you use their site and any customizations (eg; expand/hide a menu) are the most commonly collected information.

With advertising platforms like Facebook or Google, they also know a huge amount of other websites you've visited and can build a profile on your likes/dislikes/hobbies/habits and make very accurate guesses about tons of other stuff like gender/age/family/religion/race/education. If you use Google services like Gmail, when you run your google search Google also knows you bought $80 worth of Steam games during the Summer Sale last year (and no, that's not exaggeration. I forget exact details, but a couple years ago there was a huge row about google doing something like "you own this game" in the search results by pulling Steam receipt information from your emails)

Can they for example see other email addresses

It is 100% possible, but unlikely. For instance I worked with an ecommerce site where ANY email address you typed into the site (whether it be logging into your account, newsletter signup, etc) was [knowingly] collected by a 3rd party and the address was used to send "abandon cart" emails among other things. That type of thing 100% possible and semi-common. However, someone like google collecting "outside" email addresses would likely get them into trouble and isn't something I would personally be concerned about as long as you avoid Gmail.

what programs you have installed

No, the websites can't tell what programs you have installed on your computer. Websites can only really determine what browser plugins you have installed (things like Flash, Silverlight, Java) and what Fonts you have installed. HOWEVER, Chrome itself would be completely capable of identifying absolutely anything that is on your computer. Most companies do go out of their way to assure people that they do not collect/send that type of information though.

Sidenote here: almost every software that has a "crash report" (browsers, games, Steam, etc) that allows you to upload the report; the crash report almost always includes and uploads a full list of every single program that was running when the crash occurred. That is extremely common and most people don't realize it happens.

So lets say that I browse Facebook and Youtube with a browser that has an privacy-addon. I close the browser, turn on a VPN and start browsing Nissan cars or something random. Since I'm using the same browser / computer, how likely would it be for Facebook and Google to know that I'm the same person?

EDIT: Does it even make any difference at all if I'm browsing Facebook / Youtube at the same time I'm visiting the Nissan site?

Nissan uses embedded Youtube videos on their site (I just checked). So yep, Google knows [someone] was checking out cars. Doesn't matter if you play the video or not, the thumbnail preview is still loaded from a server under Google's control and that type of call probably wasn't prevented by your privacy addon.

But yes, your question of "does google know that I'm the same person" is the right one.

Under normal circumstances, when you were first browsing YouTube's site, Google would have assigned you a Unique-ID and stored that ID in your browser with a cookie. Ideally, your privacy addon should prevent this. But lets say it didn't. No VPN in existence would save from being tracked in that case because your browser will give up your identity in the form of that Unique-ID as soon as Google ask for the ID cookie.

That Unique-ID cookie method is how the vast majority of tracking is done. Block the cookie (via settings or addon), set your browser to clear cookies when closed, or just using incognito/private browsing will prevent the vast majority of tracking because you'll continually be a "new person" with these companies. The Unique-ID cookie is used for most tracking because it is extremely simple and will catch the vast majority of visitors.

However, companies can build a profile using other methods. If and/or how much companies like Google use other methods, who knows. Even if you did know, it's a good bet you couldn't say because of an NDA.

If your profile is associated with an IP address, using a VPN would help (note that IP profiles for ad tracking are uncommon because it results in very obvious false-positive matches).

If your profile is built using "fingerprinting" (see NotToBeContrarian comment) there's not a whole lot you can do. Fingerprinting is extremely accurate at determining if two short-term "hits" are the same person. However, in terms of tracking there are two big drawbacks. 1) Your fingerprint can change quite frequently so building a profile based on one would be short-term at best. 2) The information required to build a unique fingerprint also takes quite a while to collect. Where a Unique-ID cookie takes mere milliseconds to set/check, the fingerprint tester in the above comment took nearly 30 secs to run on my machine/connection.

Your question about simultaneously browsing Youtube and Nissan: no, won't matter. Both sites receive too much traffic so you'd have to use another tracking method in addition to the timestamp making the timestamp part pretty much irrelevant.

My recommendations: run your privacy addon(s). I personally am a fan of also setting the browser to "Clear cookies/local data when I quite the browser" then whitelisting the sites you log into like Voat. Protect yourself from the majority of the low hanging tracking but beyond that I wouldn't worry too much. It is a deep deep rabbithole and there is no true anonymity even if you are completely offline.
